items.title: Elizabeth I owned around 80 wigs and 2,000 dresses
items.claim: Elizabeth I's image — the painted face, the wigs — was carefully constructed. How extensive was the wardrobe?

options.text: A handful of ceremonial robes for state occasions only
Inventories at her death (1603) recorded around 2,000 gowns and roughly 80 wigs, with ceruse make-up to mask smallpox scarring from 1562
She refused jewels and dressed plainly throughout her reign

items.reveal:
Elizabeth survived smallpox in October 1562 with scarring on her face and neck. She used ceruse (white lead and vinegar) to whiten her skin — slowly poisonous.

Nicholas Hilliard's 'Treatise Concerning the Arte of Limning' notes that after about 1590 painters were instructed not to show shadow on her face — the 'Mask of Youth' image. The wardrobe was a political instrument: gifts from courtiers carried specific meanings.
items.why: Elizabeth's reign was a sustained exercise in image management. The 'Gloriana' iconography was deliberate state branding, not personal vanity.

items.title: Britain ran on local solar time until the railways forced standardisation
items.claim: When did Britain adopt a single national time?

options.text: Railway companies adopted Greenwich Mean Time from 1840 (Great Western) to coordinate timetables; legal national time followed by the Definition of Time Act 1880
Not until the 1950s when broadcasting required it

items.reveal:
Before railways, towns kept local solar time — Bristol was about 10 minutes behind London by the sun. Railway timetables made this unworkable. The Great Western Railway adopted GMT in 1840; most railways followed by 1848.

Local authorities resisted; the Exchange Clock at Bristol famously had two minute hands. The Definition of Time Act 1880 standardised legal time. The International Meridian Conference (Washington, 1884) set Greenwich as the prime meridian for the world.
items.why: The 'natural' experience of time is local. Industrial systems forced its standardisation — the railway is one of the first technologies to remake the perception of time itself.
